Customs Amendment (China-Australia Free Trade Agreement Implementation) Bill 2015 and related bill - Second Reading - Agree with bills' main idea

The majority voted against [amendments](http://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?gid=2015-11-09.184.1) introduced by Greens Senator [Peter Whish-Wilson](https://theyvoteforyou.org.au/people/senate/tasmania/peter_whish-wilson) (Tas), which means the amendments were unsuccessful. ### What were the amendments? Read Senator Whish-Wilson's [explanation](http://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?id=2015-11-09.22.1) of his amendments. ### What do the bills do? Together, these bills implement the [China-Australia Free Trade Agreement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China%E2%80%93Australia_Free_Trade_Agreement) into Australian law. This Agreement does not remove all tariffs, subsidies, quotas etc between Australia and China (so it's not really *free* trade), but it does create more favourable trading conditions between the two countries. Read more about the Agreement and the bills in the [bills digest](http://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/bd/bd1516a/16bd029).
Customs Amendment (China-Australia Free Trade Agreement Implementation) Bill 2015 and related bill - Third Reading - Pass the bills

The speaker introduced the enabling legislation for the China-Australia Free Trade Agreement, calling it the highest quality and most liberalising trade deal China has done with any developed country and the best for Australia in goods, services and investment, and argued that only two modest customs bills are needed with no changes to migration laws, contrary to claims by the CFMEU and ETU.

The Customs Tariff Amendment (China-Australia Free Trade Agreement Implementation) Bill 2015 was moved for a second reading, proposing duty-free access for certain Chinese-originating goods upon entry into force, preferential tariff rates phased to zero over three or five years for items including plastics, rubber, paper, textiles, clothing, footwear, base metals, and excise-equivalent duties on alcohol, tobacco, and petroleum products.

Labor supported the China-Australia Free Trade Agreement but opposed the inclusion of an investor-state dispute settlement (ISDS) clause, citing the Philip Morris plain packaging case as an example of its abuse. The government addressed Labour's concerns with safeguards on labour market testing, wage protections, and visa conditions for overseas workers.

The China-Australia Free Trade Agreement will eliminate tariffs on 95% of Australian exports to China, Australia's largest trading partner with $160 billion in two-way trade, and opens new opportunities for Australian services providers in health, aged care, insurance and education. Labor supported the agreement after securing safeguards for Australian jobs, including labour market testing, market salary requirements and occupational licensing obligations.

The speaker supported the Customs Amendment (China-Australia Free Trade Agreement Implementation) Bill 2015, arguing that government concessions improved worker safeguards and that Labor would address exploitation of temporary visa workers if elected. He criticised Employment Minister Senator Cash for citing a discredited claim of 178,000 jobs by 2035 from the free trade agreements.

The speaker supported the Customs Amendment (China-Australia Free Trade Agreement Implementation) Bill 2015, noting it implements preferential customs rates for imports from China under rules of origin guidelines. They praised Minister Andrew Robb for securing the agreement, which was signed on 17 June 2015, and argued it will create tens of thousands of jobs and add billions to the economy, while criticising the ACTU for spending $30 million on a campaign against the agreement.

The China-Australia Free Trade Agreement will create tens of thousands of jobs and billions in economic benefits, while union claims about weakened migration conditions are false; delaying ratification would cost the agricultural sector $300 million in 2016 and financial services $4 billion and 10,000 jobs by 2030.

A motion was moved to suspend standing orders to prioritise debate on the Customs Amendment (China-Australia Free Trade Agreement Implementation) Bill 2015 and related bill from 7:30 pm to 9:30 pm on 21 October, with no divisions called during that period, allowing the House to adjourn until 9 am the next day to finish remaining speakers and pass the legislation. The speaker noted approximately 9¾ hours of debate had occurred and encouraged speakers to reduce their time to 10 minutes to accommodate all who wished to speak.

The speaker argued in favour of the China-Australia Free Trade Agreement Implementation bills, highlighting that 85% of Australian exports would become duty-free immediately, rising to 95% upon full implementation, and citing specific industry benefits: beef exports estimated to gain $273 million annually by 2024, sheepmeat tariffs eliminated within eight years, dairy tariffs phased out over four to 11 years, wine tariffs removed over four years, and grain tariffs reduced to zero immediately.

The speaker argued that the China-Australia Free Trade Agreement will deliver substantial tariff reductions for agriculture (e.g., beef tariffs of 12–25% to zero over nine years, dairy tariffs of 10–15% eliminated over four to 11 years, sheep and goat meat tariffs of 12–23% to zero within eight years) but cautioned against overstating its benefits, noting it is not a panacea and that sugar growers did not fare well; the opposition secured changes to ensure labour market testing and skills protections for Australian workers.

The speaker supported the China-Australia Free Trade Agreement and its implementing bill, highlighting tariff eliminations on beef, dairy, seafood, wool, and other products, including a duty-free wool quota of 30,000 tonnes, and condemned the CFMEU's campaign against the agreement as economic sabotage.

The speaker argued that the China-Australia Free Trade Agreement will boost service exports, particularly education, by removing 95% of remaining tariffs and adding 77 Australian private higher education institutions to China's approved list, and named Labor leaders including Bob Hawke, Daniel Andrews, and Annastacia Palaszczuk who support the agreement.

The speaker supported the Customs Amendment (China-Australia Free Trade Agreement Implementation) Bill 2015, arguing it would give Australian businesses unprecedented access to China’s 1.3 billion consumers, eliminate tariffs on 85% of goods exports immediately and 95% eventually, and benefit sectors including dairy, beef, sheep, horticulture, services, resources and manufacturing, citing specific deals such as V&V Walsh’s box-meat agreement with China’s Grand Farm and quoting National Farmers’ Federation president Brent Finlay calling the agreement a “game-changer”.

The speaker supported the China-Australia Free Trade Agreement but defended Labour's right to scrutinise its details, citing Labour's historical leadership in Australia-China relations from Gough Whitlam's 1970s visit to the 1930s union movement's support for Chinese people against Japanese invasion.

The speaker supported the Customs Amendment and Customs Tariff Amendment bills implementing the China-Australia Free Trade Agreement, arguing the deal is essential for Australia to benefit from China’s rising middle class, and highlighted bipartisan historical efforts from the Hawke-Keating and Whitlam eras toward Asian economic integration.

The China-Australia Free Trade Agreement (ChAFTA) will add $24 billion to Australia’s economy between 2016 and 2035, create thousands of jobs, and slash tariffs on beef, dairy, horticulture, wine and coal, benefiting Durack’s cattle producers, The Chia Co, and Geraldton Fishermen’s Co-operative.

The speaker argued that the China-Australia Free Trade Agreement (ChAFTA) would benefit Australia, particularly the Northern Territory, by eliminating tariffs on key exports like beef (from 10% to zero in four years) and locking in zero tariffs for gas, potentially increasing beef production by $270 million annually.

The speaker supported the China-Australia Free Trade Agreement bills, arguing Labor secured new safeguards on labour market testing, wages, and skills standards, and highlighted benefits for Western and Northern Australian exporters in agriculture, mining, and services. They also criticised the government for misstating that the agreement would remove tariffs on iron ore and LNG, which were already tariff-free.

The speaker argued that the China-Australia Free Trade Agreement is essential to eliminate high tariffs on agricultural exports—worth around $10 billion annually—and to make Australian products competitive with New Zealand's, which gained a seven-year advantage under its own 2008 agreement. The speaker also criticised union opposition as based on outdated fears, noting that Australian farms contribute 2.4% of GDP and 99% of farm businesses are family-owned.

The speaker argued that the trade agreement negotiation process is flawed and requires parliamentary involvement at an earlier stage, with less secrecy. They questioned the benefits of the China-Australia Free Trade Agreement, noting that quotas limit growth in beef, wool, and milk powder, that concessions were later granted to other countries, and that job creation claims were exaggerated, while acknowledging progress on labour issues from negotiations with Labor.

The speaker argued that the China-Australia Free Trade Agreement must pass by end of 2015 to boost trade and jobs, citing potential $300 million losses for farmers if delayed and contrasting Australia’s position with New Zealand’s dairy gains. They rejected union and Labor objections as protectionist misinformation, insisted labour-market provisions were unchanged or justified, and claimed the deal would expand services exports and lower prices.

The speaker criticised the government for falsely accusing Labor of xenophobia and racism over job safeguards, and for overstating the FTA's job creation—claiming 178,000 jobs when the corrected figure was 14,566 by 2020—and noted the government agreed to Labor's amendments requiring labour market testing, Australian pay and conditions, and licensing for 457 visa workers.

The speaker argued that passing the China-Australia Free Trade Agreement (ChAFTA) legislation will open markets of over 1.5 billion people, benefiting small and medium enterprises and services exports, and called for a complementary agreement with Hong Kong while criticising Labor's opposition as fearmongering.

Rachel Siewert This is national Anti-Poverty Week, and I am sure people are aware that it is in fact also National Carers Week. This is a week where we strengthen our understanding of the causes and consequences of poverty and hardship and, hopefully, take action to address it. We encourage research, discussion and action to combat poverty. Unfortunately, what we see here in Anti-Poverty Week is the government attempting to cut a measure that is in fact designed to help the very people that we want to help during national Anti-Poverty Week. A 2014 report by the Australian Council of Social Services shows that poverty is still a real and very significant challenge in Australia. In fact, there has been another report that they have just put out on poverty in Australia. The CEO, Dr Cassandra Goldie, says that it is unacceptable that after 20 years of economic growth our wealthy nation is going backwards in the numbers of people falling into poverty. There are 2.5 million people living below the poverty line of 50 per cent of median income. Single parents are at a very high risk of poverty, more so because they have been dumped onto Newstart and are struggling to survive. In the latest figures a third of single parents are trying to survive in poverty. People with a disability face a significantly higher risk of poverty than other people. Forty-four per cent of people with a disability live below the 60 per cent poverty line. Just yesterday St Vincent de Paul released the report _“Sick with worry…”: stories from the front-line of inequality, 2015_. They summarise the challenges of people living in poverty: a shortage of stable, affordable housing; low incomes that are not sufficient for a decent standard of living; that it is very difficult to find stable work, particularly for people struggling with poverty; and that those struggling with poverty who have a disability are even further behind the eight ball. The government reintroduced a bill to abolish the low-income supplement, arguing it was wasteful because administration costs of $19 million per year far exceeded the $2.5 million paid to around 6,000 recipients, and the supplement was no longer needed after the carbon tax repeal. Labor will not oppose the Social Security Legislation Amendment (Debit Card Trial) Bill 2015 in the House but expects the government to provide a comprehensive package of support services, operational details, and a proper evaluation before supporting it in the Senate. The trial would place 80% of welfare payments into a restricted bank account for up to 10,000 people in up to three locations, including Ceduna.

The speaker supported the cashless debit card trial for Ceduna, Yalata and Oak Valley, noting local community backing, but criticised the lack of trigger mechanisms or exemptions for participants and called for additional financial literacy, wraparound and counselling support.

The speaker apologised to gallery attendees for the delay and confirmed question time will begin at 2:30 pm, with the government ready and the rest of the day's debate unaffected. Debate will continue on the Social Security Legislation Amendment (Debit Card Trial) Bill 2015.

The speaker supported the Social Security Legislation Amendment (Debit Card Trial) Bill 2015, which would trial a cashless debit card for up to 10,000 welfare recipients in up to three communities, starting in Ceduna, to restrict spending on alcohol, gambling, and cash advances. The trial aims to reduce social harm, with 80% of payments quarantined and 20% available as cash, and will be independently evaluated.

The bill amends social security law to enable a trial of a cashless welfare card in up to three locations, including Kununurra and Ceduna, involving up to 10,000 people as a response to Andrew Forrest’s review to address alcohol abuse in Indigenous communities.

The bill introduces a 12-month cashless debit card trial for Centrelink recipients in communities with high alcohol, drug and gambling problems, with the first trial site in Ceduna, South Australia, and advanced discussions for Kununurra in the East Kimberley. The card restricts purchases of alcohol and gambling products, with 80% of payments placed on the card and 20% in cash, and has local community support.

The speaker supported the debit card trial but raised concerns about its compulsory nature, lack of opt-out provisions, and potential to stigmatise responsible welfare recipients. They argued the trial lacks independent external evaluation, complementary support services, and measures to address alcohol supply and tobacco use, citing the 2013 parliamentary report on harmful alcohol use in Indigenous communities.

The speaker argued for the Social Security Legislation Amendment (Debit Card Trial) Bill 2015, which introduces a 12-month cashless debit card trial for up to 10,000 people in three communities, with 80% of welfare payments restricted from use on alcohol, drugs, or gambling. The trial targets areas of high welfare dependence and social harm, with Ceduna and the Kimberley region as proposed sites, and aims to reduce domestic violence and welfare-fuelled substance abuse.

The speaker opposed the Social Security Legislation Amendment (Debit Card Trial) Bill 2015 as a blanket approach that only suppresses symptoms, and argued that granting private land title deeds to Indigenous Australians is the real solution—citing his own success issuing nearly 800 deeds in Queensland. He criticised alcohol bans, highlighted Andrew Forrest’s employment of 2,000 First Australians, and contrasted Cape York Peninsula’s 154,000 head of cattle with Victoria’s 4.5 million, attributing the gap to a lack of title deeds and water licences.

The speaker argued that the Social Security Legislation Amendment (Debit Card Trial) Bill 2015, which would restrict welfare payments for alcohol and gambling in Ceduna, raises complex ethical issues but should proceed as a trial if community leaders support it, and called for a Senate inquiry to address missing details on addiction services and evaluation.

The member strongly supported the cashless debit card trial, arguing it would not restrict normal purchases but would limit spending on alcohol, gambling, and illicit drugs, with 20% of welfare payments available as cash for a couple with children. He noted Moree was withdrawn from the trial due to community misinformation, confirmed welfare recipients there were about 50% Aboriginal and 50% non-Aboriginal, and cited the Ceduna trial's community resolve and a new 18-bed rehabilitation centre in Moree as part of the need for such measures.

The speaker supported the Social Security Legislation Amendment (Debit Card Trial) Bill 2015, which introduces a 12-month trial of a cashless debit card in Ceduna restricting 80% of welfare payments from alcohol and gambling, with 20% unrestricted. The speaker cited Ceduna's 4,667 sobering-up facility admissions for 4,425 residents in 2013-14 and assault hospitalisations 68 times the national average, noting community backing from the District Council of Ceduna.

The speaker argued for the cashless debit card trial in Ceduna, where 80% of welfare payments would be placed on a card that cannot be used for alcohol, gambling, or drugs. He cited 4,667 sobering-up unit admissions and a 68-times national average hospitalization rate for assault, and named community leaders including Mayor Allan Suter and Mima Smart who supported the trial.

The speaker argued that Australia has failed to make significant progress on Closing the Gap and that accepting the status quo is not working, so policymakers must try new approaches. They announced support for the new cashless welfare debit card trial, which will be tested for 12 months in locations with high welfare dependence and social harm, and commended Parliamentary Secretary Alan Tudge for his policy development.

The Social Security Legislation Amendment (Debit Card Trial) Bill 2015 was introduced to trial a cashless debit card in up to three locations, placing 80% of welfare payments onto a card that cannot be used for alcohol, gambling, or illicit drugs. The first trial site will be the Ceduna region in South Australia from February 2016, with additional supports including financial counselling and drug/alcohol assistance, and a second trial site is being considered in the East Kimberley region.

The speaker argued that the healthy welfare card trial, centred on Ceduna, is needed to address entrenched alcohol-related harm in Indigenous communities, citing 3,000 annual deaths and 65,000 hospitalisations. He announced the bill is before the Senate, with 80% of welfare payments directed to a card blocked at liquor and gambling outlets, and criticised the Australian Greens for opposing the trial and refusing to meet with Ceduna community groups.

The bill would let the government strip Australian citizenship from dual citizens who engage in terrorism-related conduct.

It creates three ways citizenship can cease: a person aged 14 or older renounces it by acting inconsistently with allegiance, loses it for fighting for a declared terrorist organisation, or the minister may determine it ceases after a terrorist-linked conviction with at least 6 years imprisonment.
The bill applies only to dual citizens to avoid statelessness, and the minister must give written notice (or try to) when citizenship ends, unless doing so could prejudice security.
The bill broadens the grounds for citizenship cessation beyond requiring a conviction for a specified offence.
It introduces a purpose clause setting out the principles behind the amendments.
It requires the minister to report on and monitor the operation of the new arrangements.
Dual citizens who are nationals of another country and engage in terrorism-related conduct.

The majority voted in favour of a [motion](http://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?gid=2015-11-30.176.1) introduced by Senator [Richard Colbeck](https://theyvoteforyou.org.au/people/senate/tasmania/richard_colbeck), which means they were in favour of considering [the bill](http://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id:legislation/billhome/r5507) quickly. In parliamentary language, the motion was: > *That the provisions of paragraphs (5) to (8) of [standing order 111](http://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Chamber_documents/Senate_chamber_documents/standingorders/b00/b20) not apply to the bill, allowing it to be considered during this period of sittings.* [Standing orders](http://www.peo.gov.au/learning/fact-sheets/standing-orders.html) are the rules that are followed in parliament about when to speak, when to vote, when to adjourn etc. If this motion hadn't passed, the Senate would have had to wait until the next period of sittings before they could discuss whether to pass the bill. In this case, the next sitting period would've been next year in 2016 (see the [Sitting Calendar](http://www.aph.gov.au/About_Parliament/Sitting_Calendar)). ### What is this bill about? **This bill relates to the policy "[For revoking citizenship of dual nationals involved with terrorism offences](https://theyvoteforyou.org.au/policies/84)".** The purpose of the bill is to remove the Australian citizenship of a [dual national](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multiple_citizenship) in certain situations, including if they fight for or serve a terrorist organisation (read more in the [bills digest](http://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/bd/bd1516a/16bd015) and [ABC News](http://www.abc.net.au/news/2015-05-27/citizenship-stripped-under-new-laws-explainer/6500280)).

The majority voted against an [amendment](http://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?gid=2015-12-03.271.1) introduced by Liberal Democratic Party Senator [David Leyonhjelm](https://theyvoteforyou.org.au/people/senate/nsw/david_leyonhjelm). In other words, the majority did *not* want to add a new [sunset clause](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunset_provision) to the [bill](http://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id:legislation/billhome/r5507). ### What is a sunset clause? A sunset clause puts a limit on how long parts of the bill (or maybe even the whole bill) can be in force without being considered again by Parliament. For example, Leyonhjelm's proposed sunset clause would have meant that the sections he mentioned would stop being law after ten years. At that point, if the Parliament wanted the sections to continue, they would have to re-introduce them. Read [Senator Leyonhjelm's speech](http://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?gid=2015-12-03.271.1) to learn why he thought a sunset clause was needed. ### What is this bill all about? The Australian Citizenship Amendment (Allegiance to Australia) Bill 2015 was moved to automatically strip dual citizens of Australian citizenship for engaging in specified terrorist conduct, fighting for or serving a declared terrorist organisation overseas, or being convicted of terrorism-related offences, with no right to reacquire citizenship.

The opposition supported the bill and its amendments, which allow revoking the citizenship of dual nationals engaged in terrorist-related conduct offshore or after leaving Australia, or convicted of serious terrorism offences, with safeguards including ministerial discretion, six-monthly reporting, and the right to appeal to the Federal Court. The amendments narrowed the bill’s scope from potentially millions of people to only dozens, aiming to balance national security with avoiding the creation of two classes of citizens.

The speaker argued that the Australian Citizenship Amendment (Allegiance to Australia) Bill 2015 is a necessary and appropriate response to rising terrorism, allowing automatic and irrevocable revocation of citizenship for dual nationals convicted of specified terrorism offences. The speaker noted that security agencies manage over 400 high-priority counter-terrorism investigations, 26 people have been charged since September 2014, around 110 Australians are fighting in Syria and Iraq, and almost 200 are enabling terrorism, and that the bill implements all 27 recommendations of the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Intelligence and Security.

The bill was improved by committee amendments to restrict citizenship revocation to serious terrorist offences with sentences of six years or more, and to apply conduct-based loss only to persons outside Australia; Labor supported the bill despite unresolved constitutional concerns, accepting the government's assurance it would withstand a High Court challenge.

The speaker argued that the Australian Citizenship Amendment (Allegiance to Australia) Bill 2015 should pass, allowing revocation of citizenship for dual nationals engaged in terrorism-related conduct, citing over 400 high-priority counter-terrorism investigations, 26 people charged in 14 months, and more than 100 Australians fighting with terrorist groups in Syria and Iraq. The speaker also proposed a new preamble for citizenship ceremonies emphasising loyalty to Australia and its laws.

The speaker argued that Labor supports national security but will not rubber-stamp government legislation, noting the bill was scrutinised by the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Intelligence and Security, which made 27 bipartisan recommendations. The bill amends the Australian Citizenship Act 2007 to allow revocation of Australian citizenship for dual nationals who serve in armed forces of a country at war with Australia, a provision originally enacted under Labor Prime Minister Ben Chifley in 1948.

The speaker argued in support of the Australian Citizenship Amendment (Allegiance to Australia) Bill 2015, which would strip dual nationals of Australian citizenship for engaging in terrorism-related conduct, including fighting for declared terrorist organisations or being convicted of specified terrorism offences. The bill applies only to dual nationals to avoid statelessness and includes provisions for automatic cessation of citizenship and ministerial discretion, citing around 110 Australians fighting in Syria or Iraq and 190 identified supporters.

The speaker accepted the modified bill after its worst excesses were constrained by the joint committee, particularly Anthony Byrne and Mark Dreyfus, but flagged deep concerns about the legal fiction of self-actuating conduct and the threat to the separation of powers. He supported amendments targeting non-state participants like ISIS and convicted terrorists, while warning against unfettered ministerial power.

The speaker supported the Australian Citizenship Amendment (Allegiance to Australia) Bill 2015, arguing that dual citizens convicted of terrorism offences or who take up arms against Australia should lose their citizenship and be deported. They noted 110 Australians fighting with terrorist groups in Syria and Iraq, and referenced local terrorist incidents in Victoria, including the Endeavour Hills police station stabbing and the Lindt Cafe siege.

The speaker argued against anti-Muslim sentiment while criticising the government's intake of 130,000 people per year from Middle Eastern countries, citing concerns about violence and lack of rule of law, but emphasised that many Muslim Australians are ordinary, hardworking citizens and that he personally owes his life to two Muslim medical professionals.

The speaker argued that citizenship is meaningful and that updating laws to strip dual citizens who fight for terrorist groups is appropriate, but criticised the government's poor process and cheap politics surrounding the Australian Citizenship Amendment (Allegiance to Australia) Bill 2015.

The Australian Citizenship Amendment (Allegiance to Australia) Bill 2015 was supported, allowing cessation of Australian citizenship for dual nationals engaged in terrorist activities. The Parliamentary Joint Committee on Intelligence and Security recommended the bill pass with finetuning and increased transparency.

The speaker criticised the government's consultation process for the Australian Citizenship Amendment (Allegiance to Australia) Bill 2015 as a "deception" and "complete debacle," noting submissions were never made public and a final report was not produced. Labor supported the bill's final version, which only allows citizenship revocation for those convicted of terrorist offences or fighting with terrorist groups overseas, but retained concerns about its constitutionality.

The speaker argued that the Australian Citizenship Amendment (Allegiance to Australia) Bill 2015 should be passed to strip dual nationals of Australian citizenship if convicted of specific terrorism-related offences, citing that up to 250 Australian citizens have departed as foreign fighters, 40–50% of Australians fighting in Syria and Iraq are dual nationals, and about 50% of convicted major terrorism offenders are dual nationals.

The speaker opposed the Australian Citizenship Amendment (Allegiance to Australia) Bill 2015, arguing it would not improve safety, would create two classes of citizens based on dual nationality, and would violate the fundamental principle that those born in Australia cannot have citizenship stripped by a minister. The speaker cited Waleed Aly’s warning against policies that play into ISIL’s strategy of dividing societies, and urged parliament not to create unequal citizenship rights.

The speaker strongly supported the Australian Citizenship Amendment (Allegiance to Australia) Bill 2015, which creates three new automatic grounds for dual nationals to lose citizenship for engaging in terrorist conduct, including fighting for or serving a terrorist organisation overseas. The speaker noted that in nine months, 23 Australian citizens had been arrested in counter-terrorism operations, with over 400 high-priority investigations ongoing, and argued the bill would allow faster action against threats.

The speaker argued the bill is likely unconstitutional, contrary to the rule of law and natural justice, and broader than claimed, as it allows automatic renunciation of citizenship for dual citizens without a criminal conviction or trial. They warned the provision could be used against anyone who leaves Australia for any reason, and that excluding natural justice and meaningful judicial review undermines citizenship and may be counterproductive.

The speaker argued in support of the Australian Citizenship Amendment (Allegiance to Australia) Bill 2015, which would strip Australian citizenship from dual nationals engaged in terrorism-related conduct. The speaker cited over 400 high-priority counter-terrorism investigations, about 110 Australians fighting with terrorist groups in Syria and Iraq, and 190 providing support, stating the bill is a necessary response to the rising terrorist threat.

The Australian Citizenship Amendment (Allegiance to Australia) Bill 2015 would allow dual citizens to automatically lose Australian citizenship for engaging in terrorism-related conduct, fighting for declared terrorist organisations overseas, or upon conviction for serious offences such as treason or espionage, with the minister able to declare terrorist organisations subject to parliamentary review. The bill is supported by the Australian Federal Police and ASIO as a measure to keep terrorist threats offshore.

The speaker supported the bill's objective of revoking citizenship from dual citizens who engage in terrorism but argued that granting the executive power to do so without a judicial step may be unconstitutional, citing Canada, New Zealand, and the United States as examples requiring judicial oversight; they also noted the government had not provided the Solicitor-General's advice on the bill's validity.

The Australian Citizenship Amendment (Allegiance to Australia) Bill 2015 automatically strips dual nationals of Australian citizenship if they engage in terrorism-related conduct, fight for a declared terrorist organisation, or are convicted of specified terrorism offences. The speaker cited over 400 high-priority counter-terrorism investigations, 26 people charged since September 2014, approximately 110 Australians fighting in Syria and Iraq, and 190 providing support.

The speaker supported the Australian Citizenship Amendment (Allegiance to Australia) Bill, which would allow revocation of citizenship for dual nationals convicted of terrorist offences, engaged in overseas conflict, or collaborating with terrorist organisations, with safeguards including the right to appeal. The speaker strongly supported the Australian Citizenship Amendment (Allegiance to Australia) Bill 2015, which would revoke Australian citizenship for dual nationals engaging in terrorism-related conduct such as fighting with terrorist groups, financing terrorism, or recruiting. They cited figures including 110 Australians fighting with terrorist groups in Syria and Iraq, 190 providing support, 400 high-priority counter-terrorism investigations, and 26 people charged since September 2014.

The speaker argued the Australian Citizenship Amendment (Allegiance to Australia) Bill 2015 needed to balance citizenship rights with counter-terrorism measures, supporting 27 amendments secured by Labor that narrowed the bill's scope, including limiting citizenship revocation to serious terrorist offences, requiring ministerial notice of revocation, and allowing appeals to the Federal Court.
